article.overview: A lunar penetrating radar (LPR) is a ground-penetrating radar designed for the Moon. It transmits short radio pulses into the ground and records the echoes returned from boundaries where the electrical properties of the material change, such as the base of the regolith, buried rock layers or buried blocks [1][2]. Flown examples are mounted on lunar rovers, so the radar builds a profile of the shallow subsurface along the rover's traverse. China's Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 missions carried LPR instruments on the Yutu and Yutu-2 rovers [1][2], and the Chang'e-7 mission lists an LPR among its rover payloads [4]. No single design defines the class, and published mass, power and performance values are not available for every instrument.
article.description: A lunar penetrating radar sends short electromagnetic pulses into the ground through one or more antennas and records the echoes that return from subsurface boundaries. Each boundary where the electrical properties of the material change, for example between loose regolith and a buried layer or rock, reflects part of the signal. The two-way travel time between transmission and reception is converted to depth using an assumed wave speed in the ground [2]. A typical lunar LPR has these functional parts: a transmitter and pulse generator producing short, wide-bandwidth radio pulses; antennas; a receiver, timing and recording system; and rover integration, which ties the radar's position, height and data timing to the rover's motion and power and data systems. The Chang'e-4 LPR uses two antenna sets. The low-frequency channel has two monopoles, each 1.15 m long and spaced 0.8 m apart, mounted at the rear of the rover and suspended 0.6 m above the ground. The high-frequency channel has one transmit and two receive bowtie antennas, spaced 0.16 m apart, at the bottom of the rover about 0.3 m above the ground, without ground contact [2]. Echo traces are recorded at fixed intervals: 1.536 s for the low-frequency channel and 0.6636 s for the high-frequency channel. At a rover speed of about 5.5 cm/s, the along-track step is about 8.5 cm and about 3.6 cm respectively [2]. The Chang'e-3, Chang'e-4 and Chang'e-7 designs all use two frequency bands. A lower band penetrates deeper but gives coarser depth resolution, and a higher band gives shallower but finer detail [2][4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar penetrating radar is to map the shallow subsurface structure along a traverse, without excavation. The Chang'e-3 LPR was described as intended to study lunar regolith thickness and shallow subsurface structure [1]. The Chang'e-4 LPR data were used to investigate the shallow subsurface of the lunar farside [2]. The Chang'e-7 mission describes topography and subsurface structure as being obtained from its cameras, laser and radar instruments, including the LPR [4]. Other applications used in planetary ground-penetrating radar, such as mapping buried rocks, crater ejecta or lava-flow layering, are plausible but were not verified for these specific lunar instruments in the sources accessed.
article.operating_principle: Radar waves travel through the ground at a speed set by the material's electrical properties. When a pulse meets a boundary where those properties change, part of the energy is reflected back to the antenna. The time for the echo to return gives the depth of the boundary once the wave speed is known. Echo strength depends on how much contrast the boundary creates and how much the material absorbs or scatters the wave. Lower frequencies penetrate further but cannot resolve thin layers, while higher frequencies resolve finer features but are attenuated more strongly with depth. For the Chang'e-4 analysis, Li et al. used an average wave velocity of 0.16 m/ns to convert travel time to depth at that site [2]. This is a site-specific analysis value, not a universal constant for lunar regolith. Rover structure and antenna coupling can create false echoes. The Chang'e-4 authors did not analyse the low-frequency data because of rover coupling and disturbance [2]. A 2022 analysis of Chang'e-3 data argues that some deep reflectors previously attributed to lunar stratigraphy are artefacts of the radar system and its interaction with the metallic rover [3].
article.scientific_importance:
Radar is one of the few ways to observe layering beneath the surface of a rover traverse without drilling. Orbital imagery shows the surface, and rover cameras and spectrometers analyse exposed material, but neither directly measures the depth of buried boundaries. An LPR therefore fills a gap between surface observations and sample analysis.

The Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 missions show that the technique can be used on the lunar nearside and farside [1][2]. The scientific value of any such profile depends strongly on calibration, rover modelling and independent constraints. The 2022 analysis of Chang'e-3 data shows how easily system artefacts can be mistaken for geology [3]. The Chang'e-7 LPR is planned to add a further rover-based subsurface dataset if it flies and operates [4].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar penetrating radar. The examples below differ in mission, frequency bands, antenna layout, development stage and published detail. Mass, dimensions and power for the flown instruments are not publicly specified in the sources accessed, so this article does not infer them from rover-level figures.

examples.name: Chang'e-3 LPR (Yutu rover)
examples.type: Flown and operated lunar rover radar
examples.status: Flown and operated at the Chang'e-3 landing site, which the sources accessed describe as landing in December 2013 [1]. Verified values from the primary instrument paper were not read in this run.
examples.channels: Two channels; centre frequencies given in secondary summaries of [1] as about 60 MHz (CH1) and about 500 MHz (CH2). Not yet confirmed against the primary paper.
examples.depth_claims: Earlier interpretations reported regolith thickness of about 30 m and crustal structure to several hundred metres. The 2022 analysis argues that some deep reflectors are system artefacts [3]. These depths are not established and should not be treated as measured values.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 LPR (Yutu-2 rover, lunar farside)
examples.type: Flown and operating lunar rover radar on the farside
examples.status: Flown and operating on the lunar farside. Values below are taken from the Science Advances instrument description and analysis [2].

low_frequency_channel.antennas: Two monopoles, 1.15 m long and 0.8 m apart, at the rear of the rover, suspended 0.6 m above the ground.
low_frequency_channel.data_status: Not analysed in [2] because of rover coupling and disturbance.

high_frequency_channel.antennas: One transmit and two receive bowtie antennas (CH2A and CH2B), spaced 0.16 m apart, at the bottom of the rover about 0.3 m above the ground.
high_frequency_channel.data_status: Only CH2B used because CH2A showed strong cross-talk.

examples.observed_depth: Radar features detectable to about 500 ns two-way travel time; roughly 40 m at the paper's average velocity of 0.16 m/ns. This is an observed result at this site, not a rated instrument limit.
examples.not_stated_in_source: Vertical resolution as an instrument specification, transmit power, sampling, mass, dimensions and power consumption.

examples.name: Chang'e-7 rover LPR
examples.type: Planned rover radar with specified design figures
examples.status: Planned. Chang'e-7 is listed as carrying five rover payloads, one of which is the LPR [4]. No confirmed launch or operation was found in the sources accessed (see historical_significance and [5]).
examples.specified_depth_resolution: Better than 15 cm for the 100-1500 MHz band; better than 2 m for the 10-110 MHz band.
examples.specified_depth: At least 40 m for the 100-1500 MHz band; at least 400 m for the 10-110 MHz band.
examples.note: These are design or specification figures, not measured performance. The bands differ from the Chang'e-4 high band (250-750 MHz), so the figures are not directly comparable with Chang'e-4 observations.
examples.not_stated_in_source: Mass, power, dimensions and antenna geometry in the text read [4].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are not publicly specified for the flown lunar penetrating radars in the sources accessed. The Chang'e-4 antenna lengths and spacings are documented [2]: the low-frequency monopoles are 1.15 m long and 0.8 m apart, and the high-frequency receive antennas are spaced 0.16 m apart. These describe antenna layout, not the instrument's enclosure or electronics size.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified for the Chang'e-3, Chang'e-4 or Chang'e-7 radars in the sources accessed. Rover-level masses must not be used as LPR masses.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power consumption is not publicly specified for the flown instruments in the sources accessed. Chang'e-7 power is not given in the text read [4].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar penetrating radar operates in vacuum, through large surface temperature changes and under fine dust and radiation. Published thermal requirements for these instruments are not publicly specified in the sources accessed. Two operational constraints are documented. First, rover coupling and disturbance degraded the Chang'e-4 low-frequency data [2]. Second, the metallic rover can create false reflections that look like subsurface structure [3]. Antenna height, separation and mounting position therefore matter as much as the radar's own electronics. The Chang'e-4 trace timing and step sizes also set how finely the radar samples the ground along a traverse [2].
article.limitations: Echoes from system or rover structures can resemble geological boundaries [3]. Deep penetration and fine resolution are achieved in different bands, so one radar profile cannot give both at the same depth [2][4]. Depth conversion depends on an assumed wave velocity, which must be justified for each site [2]. A rover radar records a one-dimensional profile along its traverse, so subsurface structure away from the track is inferred rather than measured. Mass, power and dimensions are not publicly specified for the flown instruments in the sources accessed, and the Chang'e-7 specifications are design figures only.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A lunar penetrating radar on a rover is a surface payload. The relevant steps are integration with the rover on Earth, including antenna mounting and electrical and thermal interfaces; launch of the spacecraft; transfer to the Moon; landing or delivery of the rover system; release of the rover; and traverse operation with power and data supplied through the rover.
transportation_process: Integrate the radar with the rover on Earth, including antenna mounting and electrical and thermal interfaces.
Launch the spacecraft on a launch vehicle.
Transfer the spacecraft to the Moon.
Land or deliver the rover system.
Release the rover from the lander.
Operate the radar along the traverse with power and data supplied through the rover.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Chang'e-3 rover, Yutu, is described as released from the Chang'e-3 lander [1]. The Chang'e-4 LPR antennas are mounted at the rear and bottom of Yutu-2, at specified heights above the ground [2]. The Chang'e-7 LPR exchanges data with the lander platform through the rover's payload manager [4]. Rover stowage, release and mechanical interfaces for the Chang'e-7 LPR are not described in the text read [4].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Chang'e-3 (Yutu) and Chang'e-4 (Yutu-2) are the flown examples. Their mounting details describe these rovers rather than a general interface standard.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with any lander or rover other than the missions named above is asserted. A new LPR would need its mass, dimensions, antenna geometry, power, data and thermal interfaces compared with verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: The Chang'e-3 rover carried one of the first lunar surface penetrating radars, which was used to study regolith thickness and shallow subsurface structure [1]. The Chang'e-4 LPR extended this work to the lunar farside, and the published analysis provides a verified record of its configuration and observed depth [2]. The Chang'e-3 depth claims have been challenged. The 2022 analysis showed that deep reflectors can arise from system and rover artefacts [3]. The Chang'e-7 LPR is planned as a further rover radar with specified design figures [4]. Launch reports for Chang'e-7 are inconsistent: several summaries describe a 2026 launch that was delayed, and others give a 2027 date [5]. No launch or LPR operation was confirmed in the sources accessed.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The main uncertainties concern the status of the Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-7 instruments, the interpretation of radar echoes, and the absence of published engineering data. Values from the sources are kept separate from unverified or target figures.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image objects are included because no direct image asset could be verified for this article.

data_quality_notes: No images are included. No direct image asset URL was verified from an official or institutional page in this run, and the image rule forbids inventing one. Candidate source pages for later image research: Science Advances DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aay6898 (Chang'e-4 LPR figures, licensing to be checked), and NCBI PMC figure pages for the same paper. The PMC figure page could not be parsed for an image URL.
The Chang'e-3 LPR channel frequencies (about 60 MHz and 500 MHz) come from secondary summaries of Fang et al. (2014). The primary paper was not opened in full, so these values are unconfirmed.

The Chang'e-3 depth claims (about 30 m regolith; several hundred metres crust) are contested by the 2022 arXiv analysis, which argues that some deep reflectors are system artefacts. They are not used as established values.

The Chang'e-4 LPR values (frequency bands, antenna geometry, trace intervals, step sizes, observed depth) are taken from Li et al. (2020) as read through the PMC full-text fetch. Mass, power, dimensions, transmit power, sampling and vertical resolution are not stated there and remain null.
The Chang'e-4 observed depth of about 40 m is derived from a travel time of 500 ns and an average velocity of 0.16 m/ns. It is an observed result at that site, not a rated instrument limit.

The Chang'e-7 LPR parameters (100-1500 MHz and 10-110 MHz bands; depth resolution and depth figures) come from the rover specification table as reported in the National Science Review text read by the fetch. They are specification figures, not measured performance. Mass and power are not stated in the text read.

Chang'e-7 launch status is unresolved. Search summaries from around August 2026 describe a planned or delayed launch, and some listings give a 2027 date. No launch or LPR operation was confirmed in the sources accessed.
The Wikipedia reference is a secondary launch-status summary that was not opened in full. It is included only to record that the sources conflict.

The Fang et al. (2014) reference was identified through citing papers and an ADS record that could not be fetched (HTTP 405). Its bibcode and volume/page details are as given in citing papers; the volume was reported inconsistently (12 and 14) and is recorded here as 14(12) following the companion-paper pattern.
Lunar landing sites and location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
No lander or rover compatibility is asserted beyond the Chang'e-3, Chang'e-4 and Chang'e-7 rover contexts described in the sources.
